what_it_does: A precise exception is a guarantee that when something goes wrong during program execution (a division by zero, a memory fault, a hardware interrupt), the processor stops at exactly the right instruction and leaves all previous instructions' effects visible — as if execution happened strictly one step at a time. This guarantee is well understood for processors that follow a simple sequential model, but modern chips like Arm processors allow memory operations to complete out of program order (relaxed memory) to improve performance, which blurs the meaning of 'exactly the right point.' This paper develops a formal mathematical model — a set of rules expressed as logical axioms — that precisely defines what a correct exception must look like in the presence of relaxed memory, covering edge cases such as external hardware errors and software-triggered interrupts. A test suite of small programs (litmus tests) is also provided so future chip designers can check their implementations. This is from the abstract only.
